theme: The curses of disobedience, the weight of covenant
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 28:15-68. This is the longest and most sobering passage in the book. It describes the curses that will fall on Israel if they break the covenant. Read it carefully, and notice what is at the heart of the list.
settingTheScene: The blessings of 28:1-14 take only fourteen verses. The curses take fifty-four. Moses is not trying to scare the people but to make sure they understand how serious the covenant is. The curses begin with general disaster and grow to include defeat, siege, famine, disease, and finally exile. The chapter is the most detailed warning in the Old Testament, and the prophets will return to it again and again.
observation: “But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD your God or be careful to do all his commandments… then all these curses shall come upon you” (28:15).
“Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field” (28:16-19).
The LORD will send confusion and frustration in all that you undertake (28:20).
The LORD will strike with disease, drought, and defeat before enemies (28:21-26).
“You shall be driven mad by the sight that your eyes see” (28:34).
A foreign nation will devour the land, and a siege will cause such hunger that people eat their own children (28:49-57).
“The LORD will scatter you among all peoples, from one end of the earth to the other” (28:64).
“Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies” (28:47-48).
interpretation:
Read this passage slowly, and do not rush to explain it away. It is meant to be heavy. The curses mirror the blessings, point for point. Where the blessings spoke of rain, harvest, and victory, the curses speak of drought, blight, and defeat. The pattern says that the covenant is real, and that its terms are real. To live apart from God is to lose the goods that he gives.

The turning point is verse 47: “Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things.” The root of the failure is not a dramatic act of rebellion. It is ingratitude. A people who have everything do not thank the giver. The loss of joy in God comes before the loss of everything else.

The curses also include a reversal of the exodus. “The LORD will bring you back in ships to Egypt… and there you shall offer yourselves for sale to your enemies as male and female slaves” (28:68). The people who were rescued from Egypt are sent back into slavery. The covenant that gave them freedom, if broken, takes it away. It is a chilling statement of what covenant unfaithfulness means.

The curses are fulfilled in Israel’s history. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria, and Judah fell to Babylon. The prophets saw the exile as the working out of these very words (see 2 Kings 17 and Daniel 9:11-13). The curses were not idle threats. They happened.

Yet this is not the end of the story. Deuteronomy 30 will promise that, after the curses, God will bring his people back if they return to him. The book of Deuteronomy is balanced between warning and hope, and the warning exists in order to bring people to repentance.
connection: Paul says that “all who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (Galatians 3:10), quoting Deuteronomy 27:26, and then that “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Jesus took the covenant curses on himself at the cross: the darkness, the thirst, the abandonment, and the cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ.
application:
Read the passage as a measure of what Christ endured on your behalf. Thank him.

Ask whether there is a lack of joy and gladness in your service of God. Pray for restoration.

Spend time in gratitude, naming the “abundance” that God has given you.
prayerPrompts: Thank Christ for bearing the curse in your place.
Confess where you have served God without joy.
Ask him for a grateful heart.
